hero.headline: Fatal crash on Donald Ross Road in Jupiter kills one Sunday morning
hero.body:
A single-vehicle crash on Donald Ross Road in Jupiter Sunday morning killed one person, according to Jupiter police officials. The crash happened just before 6 a.m. when the driver came over railroad tracks, lost control of the vehicle, and struck a tree, according to preliminary information from the scene.

Police confirmed one adult male died in the crash but are withholding the victim's name pending notification of next of kin.

Both eastbound and westbound lanes of Donald Ross Road between Military Trail and Alternate A1A were closed for several hours as crash investigators worked the scene. The roadway has since reopened to traffic.

The Jupiter Police Department is continuing to investigate the circumstances that led to the fatal crash.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds defends Trump Iran conflict as necessary despite no new wars pledge
cards.teaser: Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds says President Donald Trump made the right call to stop Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, defending actions that some say contradict Trump's campaign message about avoiding new wars.
cards.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds defended President Donald Trump's actions against Iran on Newsmax's Sunday Agenda, arguing they do not contradict Trump's campaign pledge to avoid foreign wars. Donalds said the administration had to address Iran's uranium enrichment program and its development of weapons-grade nuclear material. He characterized Iran as unlike other nations and emphasized that the conflict is not endless, noting it has lasted three months with much of it occurring under a ceasefire. Donalds also claimed Iran lied about its ballistic missile capabilities, stating the weapons have a 4,000-mile range, twice what was previously claimed, and are capable of reaching Europe and U.S. bases there.

On NBC's Meet the Press with Kristen Welker, Trump said he did not guarantee avoiding war and stated he dislikes endless wars. He described the conflict as not endless and said the administration has been dealing with it for three months. Trump credited a blockade as being effective and said the threat is largely over. During his Newsmax appearance, Donalds argued that Iran's theocratic dictatorship cannot be trusted over the past 47 years because it is committed to radical Sharia law, which he said is incompatible with Western civilization.

cards.headline: Trump dismisses claims that Iran war contradicts campaign pledge to avoid new conflicts
cards.teaser: President Donald Trump says he never guaranteed there would be no wars if he returned to office, defending his decision to launch military action against Iran earlier this year.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump dismissed claims that his decision to launch war with Iran this year contradicts his 2024 campaign promise of "no new wars." In an NBC "Meet the Press" interview that aired Sunday, Trump said he "didn't guarantee" there would be no wars if elected. "Why would I have built the strongest military in the world?" he said. Trump acknowledged he doesn't like endless wars but argued the Iran conflict, which began in February, is not endless after three months of fighting. He said he was "doing the world a service" and "doing our country a service" by stopping Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. However, Trump also claimed that U.S. strikes last year "obliterated" Iranian nuclear sites, a statement that contradicted his stated rationale for the ongoing military action.

Trump also defended a now-scrapped $1.8 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund" that would have compensated allies of the Republican president. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Wednesday that the Department of Justice was abandoning the plan after a judge paused it and Democrats and some Republicans expressed concerns about its lack of oversight and potential payouts to January 6 Capitol riot participants. Trump called the fund "a great idea" and said he would be "disappointed" if not approved. When asked if people who attacked police officers on January 6 should receive payouts, Trump said, "I wouldn't be inclined to say so, but I have to see it." Trump ended the NBC interview abruptly when frustrated by pushback from anchor Kristen Welker.

cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie man was arrested after allegedly chasing children with a baseball bat.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man faces arrest following allegations he chased children with a baseball bat. The incident occurred in Port St. Lucie.

Authorities arrested the man in connection with the incident. The case remains under investigation by local law enforcement.

cards.headline: Indiantown brush fire grows to 125 acres over weekend, now 99% contained
cards.teaser: A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue an.
cards.body:
A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Forest Service. The incident started on Friday, June 5, when firefighters responded to a rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard just before 3:30 p.m. Crews quickly contained the blaze at approximately 37.8 acres, with no reported injuries and no structures threatened at the time. The Florida Forest Service assisted by establishing plow lines to help stop the spread of flames, while Martin County Fire Rescue's drone team identified remaining hotspots and confirmed full containment before crews cleared the area.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation escalated significantly when crews returned to battle a much larger 120-acre brush fire in the same general area. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident. Shifting winds and dense vegetation contributed to rapid fire growth, prompting a large-scale response from Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Forest Service, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Firefighters worked to protect nearby structures as smoke spread across the area. The fire had reached approximately 125 acres in total size and is 99% contained as of Sunday morning. Early indications suggest the fire may have been a holdover fire, with a lightning strike potentially smoldering underground before igniting visible flames. The investigation into the fire's origin remains ongoing.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie 9-year-old launches junior chess club at Fenn Center
hero.teaser: Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, launched a new juniors chess club to share his love of the game with his community. More than 36 juniors have already joined.
hero.body:
Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, is the driving force behind a new juniors chess club that launched in the city. Baptiste's love of the game began at age 5, playing alongside family. More than 36 juniors have already joined at the Port St. Lucie location. The Atlantis Chess Club now meets there every Friday.

Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, said she hopes chess will help develop the next generation. The club will help to build leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision making, Kempton said. The club is attracting players of all skill levels.

The club will soon begin two more programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. Thomas Furlong, a father who brought his children to the club, said the setting is ideal for his family. Francesca Furlong, one of the club's newest members, said she likes playing with other kids.

cards.headline: Pride on the Block raises funds for Transpire Help in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: Pride on the Block filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a non-profit providing services to LGBTQ+ individuals.
cards.body:
A vibrant celebration of love and identity filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists in support of the LGBTQ+ community. The event serves as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a non-profit organization that provides crucial services including substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals. Donna Weinberger, founder of Transpire Help, said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated. "People can come and be filled with unity and joy and happiness and be able to be in one spot and feel safe," Weinberger said.

For performers like Liam Chambers, the event carries deep personal meaning. Chambers credits Transpire Help with helping turn his life around. "I am three years sober and now I can get on the stage, I'm a drag king and I wouldn't have been able to do it without them," Chambers said. Weinberger said the fundraiser is more important than ever, as cuts to government funding have slashed the number of people the organization can help in half. "A big part of our community and especially gender diverse folk do not have health insurance or funds so they wouldn't be able to access treatment," Weinberger said.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration at Palm Beach State College
cards.teaser: 35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit.
cards.body:
Thirty-five students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit. ChildNet supports foster children and young adults through education, adoptions and independent living resources.

Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and turned to ChildNet for support. Diaz is enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College with hopes of becoming a doctor. Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber. Both shared messages of determination with others in similar situations. "Belief that you're going to be big one day and just put effort into it, never give up on school and never give up on dreams. If you like push past with the pain and just keep trying hard," Diaz said. Saintfort reinforced the message, saying "Believe that you'll make it, then you're gonna make it and stuff." Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, reflected on the evening's significance. "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard. We are to celebrate them!" Rein said.

A Fort Pierce pastor has been charged with child neglect after youngsters in her care were found in deplorable conditions, according to reports. The case involves multiple children who were under the pastor's supervision.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties for rainy season
hero.teaser: A ban on fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen takes effect June 30 across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties to reduce nutrient runoff during the rainy season.
hero.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have a ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen that takes effect June 30. Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County said the ban is to help reduce nutrient rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms. Those blooms could disrupt waterways like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River.

Skaggs said harmful algae blooms can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health.

Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, said a good alternative during the ban is using composting for your garden and landscaping. Ricketts said a small trash can is the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to your landscape.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island faces erosion so severe ocean could breach Peck Lake and split island in half
cards.teaser: A state report warns that Jupiter Island's entire 11.5-mile shoreline is critically eroded, threatening a breach at Peck Lake that could split the barrier island in two.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater to survive and could create more vulnerable coastal marshes.

According to the report, the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000 to 4,000-year-old archaeological site, is already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges like Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. There are over 33 threatened and endangered species in those areas. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project. About $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year. Field said if the island were to breach, repairs could require massive state and federal investment.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance swamped by demand as families struggle to afford housing
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives about 600 applications in the first couple hours each month, far exceeding the nearly $2 million in available funding.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program, designed to help residents who can't pay rent. The demand far outweighs available resources. Applications open at the beginning of each month but fill quickly, with the county typically receiving about 600 applications in the first couple of hours they're open. According to program director Dr. James Green, there are nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month combined with 211. The county currently has about 800 applications in the queue for rental assistance. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

Rising rental prices have pushed many Palm Beach County residents to financial hardship. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who recently moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa, spent 12 years as an educator before switching to real estate hoping for higher income. She said she worries about paying rent almost every day. Green said preventing homelessness depends on everyone and is calling on people with extra housing to partner with the county to help neighbors in need. For those who cannot get into the county's program, 211 is another important option available 24/7.

cards.headline: Florida could ban Fourth of July fireworks for 250th anniversary due to severe drought
cards.teaser: State officials are considering a statewide fireworks ban for the Fourth of July as Florida faces drought conditions more severe than 1998, the last time such a ban was enacted.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services is monitoring severe drought conditions as state leaders consider banning fireworks for the Fourth of July's 250th anniversary celebration. The current drought is more severe than 1998, the last time Florida implemented a statewide fireworks ban. The entire state is at least abnormally dry, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning in May about the possibility of a ban. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said. He acknowledged the significance of the 250th anniversary but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, owner Bill Murphy reported increased customer activity as people shop early. Murphy said the store monitors the drought index to ensure the ground is saturated enough, though he noted rain remains in the forecast. The Department of Agriculture characterized a fireworks ban as a last resort.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart, claiming she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee.
cards.body:
A woman from Okeechobee County claims she and her daughter found live worms in their SpaghettiOs and developed parasitic infections after eating the product. Mary Hubbard purchased the SpaghettiOs at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee in June 2024. According to her attorneys, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food and documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the product.

Hubbard's lawsuit seeks $50,000 in damages and alleges that Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Florida shark dive operators fight federal feeding ban, say it could devastate conservation tourism
cards.teaser: Florida shark diving operators are pushing back against H.R. 3831, the Safe Florida Seas Act, which would ban shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of the state.
cards.body:
A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is facing sharp opposition from the state's shark diving industry. The measure, H.R. 3831, also known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said Congress has not asked the industry to present data or explain their practices. Campbell is requesting the chance to speak and share the science and facts before any ban takes effect.

Industry operators say they differ fundamentally from fishing practices by avoiding surface chumming and instead taking bait underwater during dives, arguing this is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Campbell pointed to Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as a cautionary tale, noting shark incidents have increased since that ban. He is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition begins in Vero Beach to make way for mixed-use development
cards.body:
Demolition work began this week at the Indian River Mall as crews started taking down the Macy's building and the former Sears location. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager overseeing the redevelopment, said this demolition represents the first phase of a larger revitalization effort for the shopping center.

Neighbors gathered in the mall's parking lot to watch the demolition work. Mary Alice Stopyra, a nearby resident, expressed support for the project, saying the building had degraded over time. Mark Manera, another Vero Beach resident, described the mall's condition as resembling "a graveyard" after witnessing "a steady decline year after year after year" during his visits. Despite his assessment, Manera voiced optimism about the change, stating that if the project brings "new life, new jobs, new opportunity, that's wonderful." Scarfone said the revitalized site will feature a sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with approximately 300,000 square feet of retail space, restaurants, and possible residential units. He characterized the transformation as "a city within a city," noting that residents will no longer see "a dead mall for the last 12 years that was getting cobwebs." Scarfone said he hopes the first phase will be completed by 2027, with the project team still working on permitting for subsequent phases.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie 9-year-old launches junior chess club at Port St. Lucie library
hero.body:
A 9-year-old Port St. Lucie resident has started a new chess club for young players in the community. Orion Jean Baptiste created the club to share his passion for the game with others in the area. The initiative has already attracted more than 36 junior members who gather every Friday at the Port St. Lucie library. The organization, called the Atlantis Chess Club, plans to expand with two additional programs launching at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce.

Baptiste developed his interest in chess at age 5 while playing with family members. His goal now is to introduce more young people to the game and help them appreciate board games. "I just wanted kids to learn about chess," Baptiste said. He believes there is too much focus on technology among young people. "Everybody's more focused on like tech stuff," Baptiste said. "I'm hoping that more people have respect for board games."

Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, sees chess as a valuable tool for developing young minds. She believes the game teaches important life skills that will benefit the next generation. "It will help to build leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision making," Kempton said. The club welcomes players with varying levels of experience, from beginners to more advanced players.

Parents are responding positively to the opportunity. Thomas Furlong brought his children to join the club and praised the environment it provides. "This is like the perfect chance for her to learn chess, my son to get better at chess and then them to have a little sibling rivalry competition," Furlong said. His daughter Francesca, a new member of the club, finds the social aspect most appealing. "I like playing with other kids," Francesca said. The club continues to demonstrate that traditional games like chess remain engaging and valuable for young people seeking an alternative to digital entertainment.

hero.headline: 80-mile ocean paddle race to land at Lake Worth Beach June 13 to benefit cystic fibrosis families
hero.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean this June to raise awareness and funds for families living with cystic fibrosis in the ann.
hero.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean this June to raise awareness and funds for families living with cystic fibrosis in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. Participants will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. The endurance trek benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, which event founder Travis Suit established in honor of his daughter, Piper, diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule, beginning June 10, with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and a community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night.

All paddlers are required to wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held. Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, and crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31.

Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to cheer paddlers during a daylong beach celebration marking their arrival. Suit, an avid paddler, was inspired to create the event after learning about the natural respiratory benefits of ocean salt air. The foundation has since grown to provide direct support for cystic fibrosis patients and families, connecting them with resources and community. More information, registration, and donation details are available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

cards.headline: Beetlejuice musical runs through June 7 at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: The Broadway hit brings spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to Palm Beach County with performances through today at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall.
cards.body:
Rewritten Card Body

"Beetlejuice" the musical has landed at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach, running June 2 through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. The Broadway hit brings spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to Palm Beach County, with actor Ryan Stajmiger stepping into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon from Tim Burton's 1988 film. "I've loved the movie since I was a kid. I'm a huge Tim Burton fan, and you know, Michael Keaton's performance is so iconic," Stajmiger told WPTV. Though Keaton appears in the film for only 15 minutes, his impact has lasted. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a "strange and unusual" teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is breaking the fourth wall to connect directly with the audience. Early in the run, he experienced an unexpected moment when a wig change went awry. "I have a wig change on stage that I'm wearing two wigs. The second wig came off with the first wig, so I was bald for an entire scene, and I got to play with that a little bit," he explained. Performances run at 7:30 p.m. on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening shows on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up with parental discretion advised.

hero.headline: DeSantis appoints five trustees to St. Johns River State College board
hero.teaser: Five people were appointed or reappointed to the St. Johns River State College District Board of Trustees, with two new appointments and three returning members.
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis has announced appointments and reappointments to the St. Johns River State College District Board of Trustees. Alexandria Hill and Kevin Payne are newly appointed to the board, while Richard Komando, Willard "Judd" Sapp Jr., and Tammy "Chereese" Stewart have been reappointed. The Florida Senate must still confirm these appointments. St. Johns River State College operates three campuses across Orange Park, Palatka, and St. Augustine, serving approximately 8,000 students combined.

Hill maintains an active presence in the Clay County community as a member of the Clay County Development Authority. She is a partner at the Driver, McAfee, Hawthorne and Dibenow law firm. Hill earned a bachelor's degree in finance and marketing from Stetson University before obtaining her law degree from the University of Florida. Payne serves as Senior Manager of Contracting for Imagine 360 health insurance company and holds the position of President of the Jacksonville Association of Health Underwriters. He completed a bachelor's degree in accounting at the University of Texas and earned a master's degree in business administration from Oklahoma City University.

Komando brings substantial legal and judicial experience to the board as a partner in the Bradley, Garrison and Komando law firm. He has served as Circuit Director and Statewide General Counsel for the Fourth Judicial Circuit Guardian ad Litem Office for Northeast Florida and previously worked as an Assistant State Attorney in that circuit. Komando holds a bachelor's degree in criminal justice and a master's degree in business administration from Florida State University, along with a law degree from Loyola University. Sapp is involved in railroad contracting through Sapp Son Inc., based in Baldwin, and is a Navy veteran who previously served as a member of the St. Johns County Day School Board of Trustees. He obtained his bachelor's degree from Florida State University.

Stewart currently serves as Assistant County Manager for the Clay County Commission, a position she previously held as an elected member. She is active in multiple community organizations including the Clay County Development Authority, the Clay County Cattlemen Association, the Clay County Farm Bureau, and the Florida Planning and Zoning Association. Stewart earned her bachelor's degree from Texas A&M University and completed a master's degree in educational leadership and administration from the University of North Florida. All five appointees bring experience in law, business, public service, or community leadership to the college board.

cards.headline: Florida inducts five officers into Law Enforcement Hall of Fame in Tallahassee ceremony
cards.teaser: Five law enforcement officers were inducted into the Florida Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame on Saturday during a ceremony in Tallahassee.
cards.body:
Five law enforcement officers were inducted into the Florida Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame on Saturday during a ceremony in Tallahassee. U.S. Representative Kat Cammack, who represents North Florida's third congressional district, presented American flags to the inductees and families of the honored officers. The inductees were Larry Corgin, Michael "Mick" McHale, the late O.L. Raulerson, the late Harrel Reid, and Daniel Slaughter. Cammack was joined by Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Mark Glass during the ceremony.

Corgin is the retired Assistant Chief of the South Miami Police Department who served for nearly 40 years and volunteered to support New York City police in the days immediately following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. McHale is a retired sergeant with the Sarasota Police Department who serves as President of the National Association of Police Organizations. Raulerson was the only person elected sheriff in two different Florida counties, serving Highlands and Okeechobee counties over a four-decade career. Reid served as Sheriff of Hamilton County for nine consecutive terms, making him the longest serving sheriff in state history at 36 years. Slaughter is the retired Chief of the Clearwater Police Department where he had a 30-year career and helped develop the Real-Time Operations Center, noted as a model for mental health response in law enforcement.

cards.headline: Jay Collins presses Byron Donalds for debate as GOP gubernatorial primary nears
cards.teaser: Retired Green Beret and former state Senator Jay Collins is challenging Republican gubernatorial front-runner Byron Donalds to debate, comparing the Naples Congressman's refusal to former President Biden.
cards.body:
Jay Collins is pressing Byron Donalds to debate as the Republican gubernatorial primary approaches, appearing on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures to make his case. The retired Green Beret and former state Senator acknowledged his position in the field while arguing that Donalds cannot hide from direct engagement. "You can't hide in the shadows. You can't pull a Biden and hide in a corner behind your couch in the basement," Collins said. "If you're that far ahead, then what are you scared of? Step up, communicate, show up at a debate stage."

The fundamental obstacle for Collins and other challengers is the gap in resources and viability. Donalds has raised roughly $81 million during his campaign. Through reports covering activity through the end of March, Renner had raised more than $6 million and Collins roughly $1.75 million. Donalds argues that Republicans need to unite behind him rather than squander time on internecine warfare, but Collins counters that the Republican Party of Florida set criteria no one has seen. "Last I checked, we don't coronate people in America. There was a whole 1776 thing about that," Collins said. Polls reflect the financial disparity, with Donalds up big in every survey of the race.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds defends Trump Iran conflict as necessary despite no new wars pledge
cards.teaser: Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds says President Donald Trump made the right call to stop Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, defending actions that some say contradict Trump's campaign message about avoiding new wars.
cards.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds defended President Donald Trump's actions against Iran on Newsmax's Sunday Agenda, arguing they do not contradict Trump's campaign pledge to avoid foreign wars. Donalds said the administration had to address Iran's uranium enrichment program and its development of weapons-grade nuclear material. He characterized Iran as unlike other nations and emphasized that the conflict is not endless, noting it has lasted three months with much of it occurring under a ceasefire. Donalds also claimed Iran lied about its ballistic missile capabilities, stating the weapons have a 4,000-mile range, twice what was previously claimed, and are capable of reaching Europe and U.S. bases there.

On NBC's Meet the Press with Kristen Welker, Trump said he did not guarantee avoiding war and stated he dislikes endless wars. He described the conflict as not endless and said the administration has been dealing with it for three months. Trump credited a blockade as being effective and said the threat is largely over. During his Newsmax appearance, Donalds argued that Iran's theocratic dictatorship cannot be trusted over the past 47 years because it is committed to radical Sharia law, which he said is incompatible with Western civilization.

cards.headline: Trump dismisses claims that Iran war contradicts campaign pledge to avoid new conflicts
cards.teaser: President Donald Trump says he never guaranteed there would be no wars if he returned to office, defending his decision to launch military action against Iran earlier this year.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump dismissed claims that his decision to launch war with Iran this year contradicts his 2024 campaign promise of "no new wars." In an NBC "Meet the Press" interview that aired Sunday, Trump said he "didn't guarantee" there would be no wars if elected. "Why would I have built the strongest military in the world?" he said. Trump acknowledged he doesn't like endless wars but argued the Iran conflict, which began in February, is not endless after three months of fighting. He said he was "doing the world a service" and "doing our country a service" by stopping Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. However, Trump also claimed that U.S. strikes last year "obliterated" Iranian nuclear sites, a statement that contradicted his stated rationale for the ongoing military action.

Trump also defended a now-scrapped $1.8 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund" that would have compensated allies of the Republican president. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Wednesday that the Department of Justice was abandoning the plan after a judge paused it and Democrats and some Republicans expressed concerns about its lack of oversight and potential payouts to January 6 Capitol riot participants. Trump called the fund "a great idea" and said he would be "disappointed" if not approved. When asked if people who attacked police officers on January 6 should receive payouts, Trump said, "I wouldn't be inclined to say so, but I have to see it." Trump ended the NBC interview abruptly when frustrated by pushback from anchor Kristen Welker.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie 9-year-old launches junior chess club at community library
hero.teaser: Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, has started a new juniors chess club that now meets at the Port St. Lucie library every Friday.
hero.body:
Orion Jean Baptiste, a 9-year-old from Port St. Lucie, launched a new juniors chess club after falling in love with the game at age 5 while playing with family. "I just wanted kids to learn about chess," Baptiste said, noting his hope that more people develop respect for board games rather than focusing solely on technology. The Atlantis Chess Club now meets every Friday at the Port St. Lucie library, where more than 36 juniors have already joined, attracting players of all skill levels.

Diana Cowan Kempton, the club's program director, believes chess will help develop future leaders. "It will help to build leaders or members that are more focused, more patient, more strategic and thoughtful in their decision making," Kempton said. Thomas Furlong brought his children to the club, calling it the perfect opportunity for his daughter to learn chess and his son to improve his skills. For Francesca Furlong, one of the newest members, the appeal is straightforward: playing with other kids. The club will soon expand with two additional programs at the Fenn Center in Fort Pierce.

cards.headline: Indiantown brush fire grows to 125 acres over weekend, now 99% contained
cards.teaser: A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue an.
cards.body:
A brush fire that began Friday in Indiantown escalated over the weekend before being brought under near-total control, according to Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Forest Service. The incident started on June 5 when firefighters responded to a rapidly developing brush fire in the 2600 block of Southwest Warfield Boulevard just before 3:30 p.m. Crews quickly contained the blaze at approximately 37.8 acres, with no reported injuries and no structures threatened. The Florida Forest Service assisted by establishing plow lines to help stop the spread of flames, while Martin County Fire Rescue's drone team identified remaining hotspots and confirmed full containment. Officials noted the fire's cause was unknown, though early indications suggested it may have been a "holdover fire," meaning a lightning strike could have smoldered underground for days before igniting visible flames.

By Saturday, June 6, the situation escalated significantly when crews returned to the same general area to battle a much larger 120-acre brush fire. Officials believe the fire rekindled from the previous day's incident. Shifting winds and dense vegetation contributed to rapid fire growth, prompting a large-scale response from Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Forest Service, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Firefighters worked to protect nearby structures as smoke spread across the area. The fire reached approximately 125 acres in total size and is 99% contained as of Sunday morning. The Florida Forest Service remains on scene monitoring conditions, and the investigation into the fire's origin is ongoing.

cards.headline: Pride on the Block fundraiser in West Palm Beach supports Transpire Help services
cards.teaser: Pride on the Block filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, which provides substance use treatment, mental health care, and housing to LGBTQ+ individuals.
cards.body:
A vibrant celebration of love and identity filled The Peach in West Palm Beach Saturday as Pride on the Block brought together neighbors, allies, and activists in support of the LGBTQ+ community. The event serves as the largest fundraiser for Transpire Help, a non-profit organization that provides crucial services including substance use treatment, mental health care, and stable housing to LGBTQ+ individuals. Donna Weinberger, founder of Transpire Help, said the event creates a space where attendees can feel celebrated and safe. "People can come and be filled with unity and joy and happiness and be able to be in one spot and feel safe," Weinberger said.

For performers like Liam Chambers, the event carries deep personal meaning. Chambers credits Transpire Help with helping turn his life around, saying he is three years sober and now performs as a drag king, which he would not have been able to do without the organization. Transpire Help's services are especially critical for those without access to traditional health care resources. Weinberger noted that a large part of the community, especially gender diverse individuals, do not have health insurance or funds to access treatment. The fundraiser is more important than ever, as cuts to government funding have slashed the number of people the organization can help in half.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County officials respond to teen takeover threat at Wellington Green Mall
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office increased law enforcement presence at Wellington Green Mall after a social media post promoting a teen takeover gained nearly 100,000 views.
cards.body:
A social media post promoting a teen takeover at the Wellington Green Mall gained nearly 100,000 views, prompting the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office to increase its law enforcement presence at the mall. Teen takeovers are large gatherings of teens at malls, beaches or parks that typically devolve into violence. The trend has been spreading across Florida, including an event in Clearwater at the end of May that resulted in widespread property damage, fights and the shooting of a 17-year-old. Shoppers at Wellington Green Mall on Friday noticed the heightened police presence. Savanna Restrepo, who was picking up her son Isaac from summer camp, said she had seen posts about the event circulating on different social media accounts. She said the visible police presence was reassuring and lets people know that law enforcement is aware of what's going on in the community.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier called the teen takeover events "unacceptable" on social media and announced a plan to investigate and prosecute those responsible. Palm Beach County Commissioner Greg Weiss said community safety is a priority but also noted a root cause: kids need something to do. Weiss pointed to community rec centers offering programming throughout the day in county facilities and cities. He acknowledged that summer camp costs can be a barrier for some families and noted that Palm Beach County offers scholarship opportunities for summer camps. Weiss emphasized that parents should know what their kids are doing and stay in contact with them.
